comments.body:
Scope correction and a conflict the fix must resolve deliberately, both found within the hour of filing.

**It is FOUR call sites, not three.** Epic 6202's S5 merged as `8629e3874aea` while I was writing this ticket and added a fourth consumer of `pct_of_cap`:

    --value "$(pct_of_cap "$docker_container_bytes" "$CONTAINER_WRITABLE_BYTES")"

So the affected set is now `docker_storage_used_percent`, `docker_buildkit_cache_used_percent`, `journal_used_percent`, and the new container writable-layer percentage. The defect is spreading by ordinary reuse, which is the expected behaviour of a shared helper and is an argument for fixing the helper rather than the call sites.

**The conflict: S5's acceptance criteria REQUIRE the clamp.** Ticket `910b-2d43-4482-4c64` AC3 reads, in part, *"percent clamped to 100"* — clamping is written into a criterion that is being verified right now, and there is very likely a test pinning it. So this ticket and that one currently disagree about whether clamping is correct behaviour.

I am deliberately NOT resolving that by intervening in S5's verification. Its AC describes what was built, the verifier's job is to confirm the built thing matches, and having it verify against a criterion I have just contradicted would corrupt a close that is otherwise sound. S5 should close as written.

**What that means for whoever fixes this ticket.** The change is not "delete two lines from `pct_of_cap`". It must:

1. Change the helper, then find and update the test(s) that pin clamping — at minimum S5's, and any equivalent for the older three metrics.
2. Amend S5's AC3 language, or record on that ticket that the criterion was superseded. A closed ticket carrying a criterion that the tree no longer satisfies is its own future confusion, and this is exactly the shape of defect that `affd-913c-3fb0-40fb` was about: a contract that existed only inside one commit and silently disappeared.
3. Re-check the four alarms' thresholds. A metric that could never exceed 100 can now do so; confirm no alarm relied on the ceiling.

**Do not read the conflict as evidence the clamp is fine.** S5's AC was written before the live overshoot was measured, and specifying a clamp is a reasonable-looking choice until you see a 5.875 GB cache against a 5.00 GiB budget publishing 100. The measurement postdates the criterion.

**Sequencing.** This ticket should not be dispatched until S5's close lands, or the two will fight over the same function and the same tests in overlapping worktrees.

compiled_state.description:
## The defect

`pct_of_cap` in `infra/scripts/observability.sh:304-309` clamps its output:

    pct_of_cap() {
      local pct
      pct=$(( $1 * 100 / $2 ))
      [ "$pct" -gt 100 ] && pct=100
      printf '%s\n' "$pct"
    }

Three metrics are derived through it, and all three exist for exactly one purpose — to show whether a
storage cap is holding:

- `docker_storage_used_percent` (line 381, against `DOCKER_BUDGET_BYTES`)
- `docker_buildkit_cache_used_percent` (line 396, against `DOCKER_BUILDKIT_CACHE_BYTES`)
- `journal_used_percent` (line 487, against `JOURNAL_MAX_USE_BYTES`)

Because of the clamp, each is **structurally incapable of reporting the one condition it is deployed
to detect**. "Exactly at the cap" and "over the cap by any amount" are the same number. The metric
goes blind precisely when it starts to matter, and it does so silently — a clamped 100 looks like a
healthy pinned ceiling, not a breach.

## Live instance, measured

Measured on the production host 2026-09-05, `docker system df`:

    Build Cache   5.875 GB   104 entries   0 active

Configured cap, `builder.gc.maxUsedSpace` = **5.00 GiB = 5.368 GB**.

So the true ratio is **~109%**. The published `docker_buildkit_cache_used_percent` reads **100**.
The overshoot — roughly 0.5 GB, about 9% — is invisible in the metric, in its alarm, and in every
dashboard downstream of it.

The other two are not currently clamped only because they happen to be under their caps right now
(`docker_storage_used_percent` ~70, `journal_used_percent` flat at 57). They carry the identical
defect and will hide their own breach the moment one occurs.

## How this misled a live operator, concretely

I am an orchestrating session that has been reading these metrics all night. I repeatedly asserted —
on epic `endowed-upset-scaup` and on bug `cyclopean-bloodshot-hoatzin` — that "the BuildKit cap IS
working, and the number is bounded because something bounds it", citing the sustained 99-100%
reading as positive evidence of health. That inference was exactly backwards: the reading was pinned
because it was CLAMPED, over a cache that was actually 9% past its budget.

Worse, `rebar-docker-buildkit-cache-high` (threshold 85, GreaterThanThreshold) was in ALARM the whole
time and I discounted it as the cap doing its job. A clamped ceiling turns a firing alarm into
something an operator reads as reassurance. The mis-reading survived four separate measurement passes
and was only caught when an agent went to `docker system df` directly.

## Why clamping is the wrong call here, not merely lossy

Clamping a percentage is defensible for a gauge whose semantics stop at full — a progress bar, a disk
that physically cannot exceed its size. It is wrong for a BUDGET, where exceeding the number is not
an impossible state but the specific failure being watched for. `builder.gc.maxUsedSpace` is a
best-effort reclamation target, not a hard wall: BuildKit can and does sit above it. A budget metric
must be able to say 109.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `pct_of_cap` no longer clamps, so a value over the cap publishes its true ratio. Proven by a
      unit test driving the function with numerator > denominator and asserting the returned value
      is > 100, plus one at exactly the cap asserting 100.
- [ ] The three call sites (docker storage, BuildKit cache, journal) publish unclamped values, and a
      test pins that each is derived through the unclamped path — so a future re-introduction of a
      clamp at any single site is caught.
- [ ] The change is checked against every consumer of the three metrics before landing: the
      CloudWatch alarms in `monitoring_autodeploy.tf` and any dashboard or doc that assumes a 0-100
      range. State explicitly whether any alarm threshold or unit needs adjusting, or why none does.
      A metric that can now exceed 100 must not break an alarm that previously could not see it.
- [ ] The live BuildKit overshoot is re-measured after the fix and the published percentage is shown
      to match `docker system df` divided by `builder.gc.maxUsedSpace` — i.e. the metric reports the
      real ratio, not 100.
- [ ] Portability: pure shell arithmetic and local tests; no CI-provider trigger.

## Testing

1. RED first: assert `pct_of_cap 5875000000 5368709120` returns a value greater than 100. On current
   main this returns exactly 100 and the test fails for the right reason.
2. Boundary: at exactly the cap the function still returns 100 (no off-by-one introduced).
3. Consumer sweep: grep every reference to the three metric names across `infra/`, `docs/` and the
   terraform tree, and record the disposition of each.
4. Mutation: re-introduce the clamp at one of the three call sites and confirm at least one test
   turns RED.

## Scope note

This is NOT the same defect as `regretful-enormous-horsefly`, which concerns `docker_unaccounted_bytes`
differencing allocated-blocks against apparent-size. That one produces a wrong NUMBER from sound
plumbing; this one produces a CENSORED number from a deliberate clamp. They are independent and both
live.
compiled_state.title: Cap-compliance percentages are clamped to 100, so the three metrics that exist to prove a cap holds cannot report that it does not — hiding a live 9% BuildKit overshoot
